questions.question: Define Wet Ash Analysis with its Procedure. / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• Wet Ashing
  • Definition (2 mark)
  • Wet ashing is a method of decomposing organic material in food samples using strong
  • oxidizing acids, typically at relatively low temperatures compared to dry ashing. This process
  • converts organic matter into inorganic mineral components, which can then be analyzed f or
  • elements like calcium, potassium, magnesium, iron, and phosphorus.
  • Procedure (3 mark)- Explain in detail

questions.question: Outline the Principle and Procedure of Gerber Method. / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• Gerber Method
  • Definition (1 marks)
  • The Gerber method is a classical and rapid method used for determining the fat
  • content in milk and milk products. It is one of the oldest and most widely used
  • methods in dairy laboratories because it is simple, quick, and does not require
  • expensive equipment.
  • Principle (2 mark)
  • The Gerber method is based on the decomposition of milk proteins by sulphuric acid,
  • which releases the fat. The fat is then separated from the rest of the sample by
  • centrifugation and its volume is measured directly in a calibrated butyrometer.
  • Procedure (2mark) – Explain each step

questions.question: Differentiate between Gram Positive and Gram Negative bacteria. / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• Differentiate between
  • Gram-positive bacteria (2.5 mark)
  • • Cell wall: Single, thick layer of peptidoglycan (20–80 nm) that stains purple.
  • • Outer membrane: Absent.
  • • Other components: Contains teichoic and lipoteichoic acids.
  • • Antibiotic resistance: Generally more susceptible to antibiotics, as the thick
  • peptidoglycan layer is easily penetrated.
  • • Toxins: Can produce exotoxins, such as neurotoxins and enterotoxins.
  • • Examples: Staphylococcus and Streptococcus.
  • Gram-negative bacteria (2.5 mark)
  • • Cell wall: Double-layered with a thin peptidoglycan layer (8–10 nm) and an outer lipid
  • membrane that stains pink or red.
  • • Outer membrane: Present, which contains lipopolysaccharides and acts as a protective
  • barrier, making them more resistant to antibiotics.
  • • Other components: Contains porins in the outer membrane but lacks teichoic acids.
  • • Antibiotic resistance: More resistant to antibiotics due to the outer membrane
  • protecting the thin peptidoglycan layer.
  • • Toxins: Can produce both endotoxins (released when the cell dies) and exotoxins.
  • • Examples: Escherichia and Salmonella.

questions.question: Describe the streak plate,spread plate and pour plate methods / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• Culture technique
  • Definition (1 mark)
  • Streak plate (3 marks)
  • • Purpose: To isolate pure colonies from a mixed culture.
  • • Method: The inoculum is spread over the surface of solid agar in streaks using a sterile loop,
  • sterilized between streaks.
  • • Result: Individual colonies appear in the final streaked area.
  • • Example: Isolation of E. coli or Staphylococcus aureus.
  • Spread plate (3 marks)
  • • Purpose: For quantitative culture and surface colony isolation.
  • • Method: A measured volume of diluted sample is spread evenly on solid agar using a sterile
  • spreader.
  • • Result: Colonies develop only on the surface.
  • • Example: Used for viable bacterial count in samples.
  • Pour plate (3 marks)
  • • Purpose: To count bacteria (colony-forming units) and obtain isolated colonies.
  • • Method: A small amount of diluted sample is mixed with molten agar and poured into a Petri
  • dish.
  • • Result: Colonies grow both on the surface and within the medium.
  • • Example: Used in quantitative microbial analysis of water or milk.
